questions.q: What is the purpose of the root cap in a plant root?
options: To protect the tender apex of the root
questions.solution: The root is covered at the apex by a thimble-like structure called the root cap (Figure 5.3). It protects the tender apex of the root as it makes its way through the soil. A few millimetres above the root cap is the region of meristematic activity. The cells of this region are very small, thin-walled and with dense protoplasm. They divide repeatedly. The cells proximal to this region undergo rapid elongation and enlargement and are responsible for the growth of the root in length. This region is called the region of elongation. The cells of the elongation zone gradually differentiate and mature. Hence, this zone, proximal to region of elongation, is called the region of maturation. From this region some of the epidermal cells form very fine and delicate, thread-like structures called root hairs. These root hairs absorb water and minerals from the soil.

questions.q: What is the role of buds in the stem?
questions.solution: The leaf is a lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem. It develops at the node and bears a bud in its axil. The axillary bud later develops into a branch. Leaves originate from shoot apical meristems and are arranged in an acropetal order. They are the most important vegetative organs for photosynthesis.

questions.q: What are the three main parts of a typical leaf?
options: Shoot apical meristems, acropetal order, and photosynthesis
questions.solution: A typical leaf consists of three main parts: leaf base, petiole and lamina (Figure 5.4 a). The leaf is attached to the stem by the leaf base and may bear two lateral small leaf like structures called stipules. In monocotyledons, the leaf base expands into a sheath covering the stem partially or wholly. In some leguminous plants the leafbase may become swollen, which is called the pulvinus. The petiole help hold the blade to light. Long thin flexible petioles allow leaf blades to flutter in wind, thereby cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to leaf surface. The lamina or the leaf blade is the green expanded part of the leaf with veins and veinlets. There is, usually, a middle prominent vein, which is known as the midrib. Veins provide rigidity to the leaf blade and act as channels of transport for water, minerals and food materials. The shape, margin, apex, surface and extent of incision of lamina varies in different leaves.

questions.q: In which type of phyllotaxy does a single leaf arise at each node in an alternate manner?

In alternate type of phyllotaxy, a single leaf arises at each node in alternate manner, as in china rose, mustard and sun flower plants. In opposite type, a pair of leaves arise at each node and lie opposite to each other as in Calotropis and guava plants. If more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl, it is called whorled, as in Alstonia.

questions.q: What is a flower?
questions.solution: A flower is a modified shoot wherein the shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem. Internodes do not elongate and the axis gets condensed. The apex produces different kinds of floral appendages laterally at successive nodes instead of leaves. When a shoot tip transforms into a flower, it is always solitary. The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is termed as inflorescence. Depending on whether the apex gets developed into a flower or continues to grow, two major types of inflorescences are defined – racemose and cymose.

A flower is asymmetric (irregular) if it cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre, as in canna.

questions.q: What is the definition of aestivation?
options: The study of plants and flowers
The study of birds and their habitats
The arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl
questions.solution: The mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl is known as aestivation. The main types of aestivation are valvate, twisted, imbricate and vexillary (Figure 5.11). When sepals or petals in a whorl just touch one another at the margin, without overlapping, as in Calotropis, it is said to be valvate. If one margin of the appendage overlaps that of the next one and so on as in china rose, lady’s finger and cotton, it is called twisted. If the margins of sepals or petals overlap one another but not in any particular direction as in Cassia and gulmohur, the aestivation is called imbricate. In pea and bean flowers, there are five petals, the largest (standard) overlaps the two lateral petals (wings) which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior petals (keel); this type of aestivation is known as vexillary or papilionaceous.

questions.q: In which type of placentation do the ovules form a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary?
questions.solution: The arrangement of ovules within the ovary is known as placentation. The placentation are of different types namely, marginal, axile, parietal, basal, central and free central (Figure 5.12). In marginal placentation the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary and the ovules are borne on this ridge forming two rows, as in pea. When the placenta is axial and the ovules are attached to it in a multilocular ovary, the placentaion is said to be axile, as in china rose, tomato and lemon. In parietal placentation, the ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on peripheral part. Ovary is one-chambered but it becomes twochambered due to the formation of the false septum, e.g., mustard and Argemone. When the ovules are borne on central axis and septa are absent, as in Dianthus and Primrose the placentation is called free central. In basal placentation, the placenta develops at the base of ovary and a single ovule is attached to it, as in sunflower, marigold.

questions.solution: A flower may be trimerous, tetramerous or pentamerous when the floral appendages are in multiple of 3, 4 or 5, respectively. Flowers with bracts-reduced leaf found at the base of the pedicel- are called bracteate.

questions.solution: Bases on the position of calyx, corolla and androecium in respect of the ovary on thalamus, the flowers are described as hypogynous, perigynous and epigynous.

Assertion: The calyx is the outermost whorl of the flower and the members are called petals.

questions.subject: Botany

questions.solution: Gynoecium is the female reproductive part of the flower and is made up of one or more carpels. When more than one carpel is present, they may be free and are called apocarpous.

questions.q:

1. In some plants, like grass, Monstera and the banyan tree, roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle and are called adventitious roots.
2. The fibrous root system is seen in the mustard plant.
3. The main functions of the root system are absorption of water and minerals from the soil, providing a proper anchorage to the plant parts, storing reserve food material and synthesis of plant growth regulators.
4. In monocotyledonous plants, the primary root is short lived.
questions.solution: The fibrous root system is seen in wheat plant. In some plants, like grass, Monstera and the banyan tree, roots arise from parts other than the radicle and are called adventitious roots. The main functions of the root system are absorption of water and minerals from the soil, providing a proper anchorage to the plant parts, storing reserve food material and synthesis of plant growth regulators.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:

1. The arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina of leaf is termed as inflorescence.
2. When the veinlets form a network, it is called the reticulate venation.
3. Leaves of dicotyledonous plants generally possess reticulate venation, while parallel venation is the characteristic of most monocotyledons.
4. parallel venation is the characteristic of most dicotyledons.
questions.solution: The arrangement of veins and the veinlets in the lamina of leaf is termed as venation. When the veinlets form a network, the venation is termed as reticulate venation. Leaves of dicotyledonous plants generally possess reticulate venation, while parallel venation is the characteristic of most monocotyledons.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Read the following statements and choose the correct option:
1. A leaf is said to be simple, when its lamina is entire or when incised, the incisions do not touch the midrib
2. When the incisions of the lamina reach up to the midrib breaking it into a number of leaflets, the leaf is called compound.
3. A bud is present in the axil or petiole in both simple and compound leaves, also in the axil of leaflets of the compound leaf.
4. The compound leaves may be of two types
questions.solution: A leaf is said to be simple, when its lamina is entire or when incised, the incisions do not touch the midrib. When the incisions, of the lamina reach up to the midrib breaking it into a number of leaflets, the leaf is called compound. A bud is present in the axil of petiole in both simple and compound leaves, but not in the axil of leaflets of the compound leaf.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Read the following statements and choose the correct option:
1. The compound leaves may be of two types- pinnately compound leaf and palmately compound leaf
2. In pinnately compound leaf, the leaflets are attached at a common point.
3. The examples of palmately compound leaves is neem.
4. in palmately compound leaf a number of leaflets are present on a common axis, the rachis.
5. silk cotton is a example of pinnately compound leaf.
questions.solution: The compound leaves may be of two types-pinnately compound leaf and palmately compound leaf. In a pinnately compound leaf a number of leaflets are present on a common axis, the rachis, which represents the midrib of the leaf, as in neem. In palmately compound leaves, the leaflets are attached at a common point, as in silk cotton.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:

3. The example of alternate type of phyllotaxy is mustard and sunflower plants
4. If more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl, it is called whorled, as in Alstonia.
questions.solution: Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch. In alternate type of phyllotaxy, a single leaf arises at each node in alternate manner, as in china rose, mustard and sunflower plants.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:

4. The seed coat has two layers, the inner testa and the outer tegmen.
questions.solution: The ovules after fertilization, develop into seeds. A seed is made up of a seed coat and an embryo. The embryo is made up of a radicle, an embryonal axis and one or two cotyledons.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:

B. Fibrous Root System2. Mustard
C. Adventitious Root System3. Banyan Tree
D. None4. Rose
questions.solution: The tap root system is exemplified by the mustard plant, the fibrous root system is seen in the wheat plant, the adventitious root system is found in the banyan tree.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Root RegionsCharacteristics
A. Region of Meristematic Activity1. Cells undergo rapid elongation and enlargement
B. Region of Elongation2. Cells are very small, thin-walled, and with dense protoplasm
C. Region of Maturation3. Cells gradually differentiate and mature
D. Root Cap4. Protects the tender apex of the root
questions.solution: The region of meristematic activity contains cells that are very small, thin-walled, and have dense protoplasm, the region of elongation is characterized by rapid elongation and enlargement of cells, the region of maturation has cells that gradually differentiate and mature, and the root cap protects the tender apex of the root.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Functions of the root systemDescriptions
A. Absorption of Water and Minerals1. Provides stability to the plant
B. Anchorage2. Enables the plant to take in essential nutrients
C. Storage of Reserve Food3. Keeps excess nutrients for future use
D. Synthesis of Plant Growth Regulators4. Produces substances that regulate plant growth
questions.solution: The absorption function enables the plant to take in essential nutrients, anchorage provides stability to the plant, storage keeps excess nutrients for future use, and synthesis involves producing substances that regulate plant growth.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Root StructuresDescriptions
A. Tap Root1. Arises from parts of the plant other than the radicle
B. Fibrous Root2. Originates from the base of the stem
C. Adventitious Root3. Originates from the radicle
D. Root Cap4. Protects the root tip as it grows through the soil
questions.solution: Tap roots originate from the radicle, fibrous roots originate from the base of the stem, adventitious roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle, and the root cap protects the root tip as it grows through the soil.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Parts of the StemDescriptions
A. Nodes1. Portions between two nodes
B. Internodes2. The region where leaves are born
C. Buds3. May be terminal or axillary
D. Plumule4. Develops into the stem from the embryo
questions.solution: Nodes are the regions where leaves are born, internodes are the portions between nodes, buds can be terminal or axillary, and the plumule develops into the stem from the embryo.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Functions of the StemDescriptions
A. Spreading out branches1. Carries water, minerals, and photosynthates
B. Conducting substances2. Provides structural support and defense
C. Storage of food3. Stores excess nutrients
D. Protection4. Supports the growth of leaves, flowers, and fruits
questions.solution: Spreading out branches supports the growth of leaves, flowers, and fruits, conducting substances involves carrying water, minerals, and photosynthates, storage of food keeps excess nutrients, and protection provides structural support and defense.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Stem CharacteristicsStages of Development
A. Green1. Young stage
B. Woody2. Function of spreading out
C. Bearing branches3. Later stage
D. Developing from the plumule4. Initial development
questions.solution: The stem is green when young, becomes woody later, bears branches to spread out leaves, flowers, and fruits, and develops from the plumule of the embryo.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Leaf PartsDescriptions
A. Leaf Base1. The green expanded part of the leaf with veins.
B. Petiole2. The structure that holds the leaf blade to light.
C. Lamina3. The part of the leaf that may bear two small lateral structures.
D. Stipules4. The part that attaches the leaf to the stem.
questions.solution: The leaf base attaches the leaf to the stem, the petiole holds the blade to light, the lamina is the green part of the leaf, and stipules are the small structures that may be present
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Venation TypesDescriptions
A. Reticulate1. Veins run parallel to each other.
B. Parallel2. Veinlets form a network.
C. Pinnate3. Primary veins radiate from a central point.
D. Palmate4. Primary veins form a branching pattern.
questions.solution: Reticulate venation has veinlets forming a network, parallel venation has veins running parallel, pinnate venation has primary veins branching out, and palmate venation has veins radiating from a central point.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Venation typeCharacteristic.
A. Reticulate Venation1. Veins run parallel to each other
B. Parallel Venation2. Veinlets form a network
C. Monocotyledons3. Characteristic of most monocotyledons
D. Dicotyledons4. Generally possess reticulate venation
questions.solution: Reticulate venation forms a network, parallel venation has veins running parallel, monocotyledons typically have parallel venation, and dicotyledons usually have reticulate venation.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Leaf PartsFunction.
A. Veins1. Provides rigidity and channels transport for water and nutrients
B. Midrib2. The central prominent vein
C. Petiole3. The green expanded part with veins
D. Leaf Blade4. Holds the leaf to the stem and can aid in cooling
questions.solution: Veins provide rigidity and transport, the midrib is the central vein, the petiole holds the leaf and can aid in cooling, and the leaf blade is the green part.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Leaf typeExample.
A. Simple Leaf1. Neem
B. Compound Leaf2. Silk Cotton
C. Pinnately Compound Leaf3. A leaf with incisions not reaching the midrib
D. Palmately Compound Leaf4. A leaf with leaflets on a common axis
questions.solution: A simple leaf has incisions not reaching the midrib, a compound leaf breaks into leaflets, a pinnately compound leaf is like the neem, and a palmately compound leaf is like the silk cotton.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Leaf typeSpecific term.
A. Leaf with incisions breaking into leaflets1. Simple Leaf
B. Leaf with incisions not reaching midrib2. Compound Leaf
C. Leaflets attached at a common point3. Pinnately Compound Leaf
D. Leaflets on a common axis (rachis)4. Palmately Compound Leaf
questions.solution: A leaf with incisions breaking into leaflets is a compound leaf, a leaf with incisions not reaching the midrib is a simple leaf, leaflets attached at a common point are palmately compound, and leaflets on a common axis are pinnately compound.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Leaf featureFunction.
A. Stipules1. May bear small leaf-like structures
B. Leaf Base2. Helps in cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air
C. Petiole3. The green part that performs photosynthesis
D. Leaf Blade4. Connects the leaf to the stem and can swell in some plant
questions.solution: Stipules may bear small leaf-like structures, the leaf base connects the leaf to the stem and can swell, the petiole helps in cooling and bringing fresh air, and the leaf blade performs photosynthesis.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Leaf modificationType.
A. Monocotyledons1. Leaves usually have reticulate venation
B. Dicotyledons2. Leaves usually have parallel venation
C. Compound Leaf3. Leaflets are not separated by incisions reaching the midrib
D. Simple Leaf4. Leaflets are separated by incisions reaching the midrib
questions.solution: Monocotyledons usually have parallel venation, dicotyledons have reticulate venation, compound leaves have leaflets separated by incisions reaching the midrib, and simple leaves have incisions not reaching the midrib.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Phyllotaxy TypesCharacteristics
A. Alternate1. A pair of leaves arises at each node, lying opposite to each other
B. Opposite2. A single leaf arises at each node in an alternate manner
C. Whorled3. More than two leaves arise at a node forming a whorl
D. Inflorescence4. The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis
questions.solution: Alternate phyllotaxy involves a single leaf per node, opposite phyllotaxy involves a pair of leaves per node, whorled phyllotaxy involves more than two leaves per node, and inflorescence refers to the arrangement of flowers on the floral axis.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Plant ExamplesPhyllotaxy Types
A. China Rose1. Whorled
B. Calotropis2. Opposite
C. Alstonia3. Alternate
D. Mustard4. Alternate
questions.solution: China Rose and Mustard have alternate phyllotaxy, Calotropis has opposite phyllotaxy, and Alstonia has whorled phyllotaxy.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Inflorescence TypesGrowth Patterns
A. Racemose1. Main axis terminates in a flower and is limited in growth
B. Cymose2. Main axis continues to grow and flowers are borne laterally
C. Floral Axis3. Arrangement of flowers on the axis
D. Floral Meristem4. Shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem
questions.solution: In racemose inflorescence, the main axis continues to grow, while in cymose inflorescence, it terminates in a flower. Floral axis refers to the arrangement of flowers, and floral meristem is when the shoot apical meristem changes to floral.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Floral Development TermsDescriptions
A. Modified Shoot1. Changes to floral meristem and does not elongate
B. Shoot Apical Meristem2. Structures produced laterally at successive nodes
C. Floral Appendages3. The part of the flower where leaves are modified
D. Internodes4. Do not elongate in floral development
questions.solution: A modified shoot turns into a flower, the shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem, floral appendages are produced laterally, and internodes do not elongate.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Floral WhorlsDescriptions
A. Calyx1. Reproductive organ that consists of stamens
B. Corolla2. Accessory organ that forms the outermost whorl
C. Androecium3. Reproductive organ that consists of carpels
D. Gynoecium4. Accessory organ that forms the second whorl
questions.solution: The calyx is an accessory organ that forms the outermost whorl. The corolla is also an accessory organ but forms the second whorl. Androecium is the reproductive organ consisting of stamens, and gynoecium is the reproductive organ consisting of carpels.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Symmetry TypesExamples
A. Actinomorphic1. Pea, Gulmohur
B. Zygomorphic2. Mustard, Datura
C. Asymmetric3. Canna
D. Cannot be determined4. Cannot be answered
questions.solution: Actinomorphic flowers have radial symmetry, as in mustard and datura. Zygomorphic flowers have bilateral symmetry, as in pea and gulmohur. Asymmetric flowers cannot be divided into two similar halves, as in canna.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Floral PositionFlower Type
A. Hypogynous1. Gynoecium at the highest position, ovary superior
B. Perigynous2. Margin of thalamus grows upward, ovary inferior
C. Epigynous3. Gynoecium in the center, ovary half inferior
D. Cannot be determined4. Cannot be answered
questions.solution: Hypogynous flowers have the gynoecium at the highest position with a superior ovary, perigynous flowers have the gynoecium in the center with a half inferior ovary, and epigynous flowers have the ovary completely enclosed by the thalamus with an inferior ovary.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Flower ArrangementDescriptions
A. Perigynous1. Gynoecium in the center, ovary half inferior
B. Hypogynous2. Gynoecium at the highest position, ovary superior
C. Epigynous3. Cannot be determined
D. Cannot be determined4. Thalamus grows upward and fuses with the ovary, ovary inferior
questions.solution: Perigynous flowers have the gynoecium in the center with a half inferior ovary, hypogynous flowers have the gynoecium at the highest position with a superior ovary, and epigynous flowers have the thalamus growing upward and fusing with the ovary, resulting in an inferior ovary.
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:
Aestivation TypesDescriptions
A. Valvate1. Sepals or petals overlap each other but not in a particular direction
B. Twisted2. Sepals or petals just touch each other at the margin without overlapping
C. Imbricate3. Largest petal overlaps lateral petals, which overlap the smallest anterior petals
D. Vexillary4. One margin of the appendage overlaps that of the next one
questions.solution: Valvate aestivation has sepals or petals just touching each other at the margin without overlapping. Twisted aestivation has margins overlapping one another. Imbricate aestivation involves overlapping in no particular direction, and vexillary (or papilionaceous) involves a specific overlapping pattern of petals
questions.subject: Botany

questions.q:

A. Calotropis1. Valvate
B. China Rose2. Imbricate
C. Cassia3. Twisted

questions.q:
Match the type of placentation in Column I with its corresponding structural characteristic and plant example in Column II.
Column IColumn II
(a) Axile(i) False septum formation in a unilocular ovary; Mustard
(b) Parietal(ii) Single ovule attached at the ovary base; Sunflower
(c) Free central(iii) Multilocular ovary with central attachment; Lemon
(d) Basal(iv) Septa are completely absent; Dianthus
Select the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.solution:
Refer: NCERT | Class 11 | Page: 65 | Paragraph: 2

Axile placentation occurs in a multilocular ovary where ovules are attached to the central axis. Example: Lemon. Thus, (a) matches (iii).

Parietal placentation occurs when ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary. A false septum may form, making the unilocular ovary bilocular. Example: Mustard. Thus, (b) matches (i).

Free central placentation features ovules borne on a central axis with septa completely absent. Example: Dianthus. Thus, (c) matches (iv).

Basal placentation involves a single ovule attached at the base of the ovary. Example: Sunflower. Thus, (d) matches (ii).

The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

Answer: (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii)
